paras: The threatened lynching of Max Hoppe took place in late May and early June 1888 in northern Montana Territory, after Hoppe was accused of shooting John Adams at a camp near Fort Conrad and pursuers from that settlement took up his trail. No lynching followed: Hoppe was held by Canadian mounted police, extradited, and sentenced at Fort Benton to twenty years for second-degree murder. The case drew a Great Falls editorial urging that 'the intention to lynch him' be abandoned for the sake of Montana's reputation.

According to the Fort Benton River Press, Augustus Brede and Adams left Fort Benton for Fort Macleod in a wagon about a week before the shooting and agreed to carry a stranger who said he was without means. The stranger was later identified as Max Hoppe, a Pole about 26 or 27 years old who worked as a traveling jeweler and had been in Helena, Butte, Great Falls and Calgary. Acquaintances in Great Falls called him 'a crazy scoundrel', and the River Press described him as 'evidently a crank'.

The three camped at Nine Mile coulee, nine miles north of Fort Conrad, and on Tuesday morning, May 29, Brede went to look for the horses while the other two stayed at the wagon. Brede returned three hours later to find Adams shot three times, and Adams said the stranger had ordered him to throw up his hands and opened fire. Adams died on the way to Fort Benton.

A Benton dispatch of June 1 reported that 'parties from Fort Conrad' were on the trail and that if caught Hoppe 'will probably be lynched by friends of the deceased'; Deputy Sheriff Charles Crawford set out separately. Hoppe reached the Sweet Grass Hills mining camps bareheaded and in a bloody shirt, where some miners proposed holding him, but he told a story about a quarrel with whiskey traders and was let go. Crawford followed the trail across the boundary and found that Canadian mounted police had already arrested Hoppe for stealing provisions; at Crawford's request they held him pending extradition.

An extradition warrant for Hoppe, then in custody at Lethbridge, was forwarded from Ottawa on August 21. Crawford brought him to the Benton jail in early September, where Hoppe told a reporter, 'What I did I did in self-defense.' At the November term of the Choteau County court Hoppe was convicted of murder in the second degree and sentenced to twenty years in the penitentiary.

Montana papers treated the shooting as 'a most cold-blooded murder', and the River Press called Hoppe a 'fiend'. The lynching forecast appeared in the Benton dispatch as printed by the Livingston Enterprise and the Great Falls Tribune, stated as a likely outcome without comment. Once Hoppe was in Canadian custody, the Tribune argued editorially that he 'should then receive a fair trial', that lynching 'disgraces and demoralizes' a community, and that 'lynching is rare in Montana'.

By contrast, the Butte Semi-Weekly Miner reported 'much regret' that the capture had not been made on American soil, since that delayed 'the demands of justice'. Outside the territory, papers in Minnesota and Dakota carried wire versions under headings such as 'Unprovoked Murder' and 'A Murderer Run Down', without the lynching line. The November court reports presented the term's convictions as proof that the county meant 'to suppress crime through the agency of the courts.'

Accounts of the motive differed: the Benton dispatch said Adams named robbery, the River Press said Adams described no cause but a wish to be 'tough', and Hoppe claimed self-defense. The slain man's first name was printed as John in the Montana papers, as Johnny in a wire version, and as William in an Ottawa dispatch.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Max Hoppe
bases: Benton dispatches said Hoppe would 'probably' or 'may' be lynched by the slain man's friends if caught, and a Great Falls editorial spoke of 'the intention to lynch him', but no mob action is reported; he was held in Canada and tried in court [A1, A3, A11, A15].

Hoppe was not killed: he was held by Canadian mounted police, extradited and sentenced to prison [A2, A14, A15]; the only lynching element is a press forecast that pursuers from Fort Conrad might lynch him in revenge for the killing of Adams [A1, A3, A11].

The killing, pursuit, extradition and conviction are reported by several independent Montana papers [A2, A5, A14, A15, A16], but the lynching threat rests on a single Benton dispatch printed in two papers [A1, A3] and one Great Falls editorial [A11].

accounts.label: Benton dispatch
accounts.gist: Hoppe shot Adams three times while Brede was away, for robbery as Adams said; pursuers from Fort Conrad were on his trail and would probably lynch him if they caught him.

accounts.label: River Press (Fort Benton), from Brede and Adams
accounts.gist: Hoppe shot Adams without provocation, declaring 'I am the father of toughs!', took a rifle and fled; he later talked his way past miners in the Sweet Grass Hills.

accounts.label: Hoppe's claim
accounts.gist: Hoppe told a reporter at the Benton jail that what he did he did in self-defense.

framing.detail: The Great Falls Tribune editorial said 'the intention to lynch him should be abandoned', calling lynching a disgrace to the community and noting 'lynching is rare in Montana'.
The Benton dispatch reported the expected lynching flatly as a likely outcome ('will probably be lynched by friends of the deceased') without comment.
Outside Montana the story ran as wire copy under heads such as 'Unprovoked Murder' and 'A Murderer Run Down', without the lynching line.

record_check.dossier: Threatened only in a press forecast and an editorial's reference to an 'intention to lynch'; no mob gathered or acted, and Hoppe went through extradition and trial.
Adams was shot Tuesday, May 29, 1888; the lynching threat was reported June 1-9.
Nine Mile coulee, nine miles north of Fort Conrad (pursuers from Fort Conrad).
Hoppe is described as a Pole, a native of Poland; no race is stated for him or Adams.
'Parties from Fort Conrad' described as 'friends of the deceased'.
At large when the threat was printed; held by Canadian mounted police from about June 2-4, then in the Benton jail from September.
Accused of shooting John Adams near Fort Conrad; later convicted of second-degree murder.

info: Adams was shot on a Tuesday morning, reported as 'Tuesday last' in a June 1 dispatch and as May 29 in a wire brief.
Nine Mile coulee, nine miles north of Fort Conrad, Montana; Adams died at Bevins' place on Pen d'Oreille coulee on the way to Fort Benton.
Max Hoppe, the threatened man, described as a Pole about 26 or 27 years old and an itinerant jeweler; John Adams was the man he was accused of killing.
Accused of shooting John Adams three times at their camp; Adams was reported to have said the shooting was for robbery, or without provocation; Hoppe said he acted in self-defense.
'Parties from Fort Conrad' on Hoppe's trail, described as 'friends of the deceased'; no group is named.
Sentenced to twenty years in the penitentiary.
